periods.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of electric current
periods.activity_description: A magnetic compass is placed beneath a current-carrying wire in a simple circuit. Students observe needle deflection when the switch is closed and its return when the switch is opened, recording both positions and sketching the setup.

roles.role_description: Assembles the circuit at the front and invites students to observe and record the needle position at each switch state.
Each group observes the compass needle, records both switch states, and sketches the arrangement of wire and needle.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up the circuit and poses the opening question: does current do anything to a nearby compass needle?
Groups conduct the observation, systematically recording needle direction with switch open and with switch closed.
Groups share observations and the class constructs a common record on the board, noting the pattern.
Teacher introduces the term magnetic field and links the observation to the idea that a current-carrying wire has a magnetic effect.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's first big idea, so orient students to the central question — can electricity produce a magnetic effect — before handing materials over. Watch for the common error of students moving the compass too far from the wire and reporting no deflection; ensure the compass is placed directly beneath the wire. A good readiness checkpoint: every group should be able to state whether the effect persists or disappears when the switch is opened.
materials: Simple circuit with battery, switch, and connecting wire

periods.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of electric current
periods.activity_description: Students wrap insulated wire around an iron nail, connect it to a cell, and test whether the nail attracts iron paper clips. They observe that clips cling when current flows and fall off when the circuit is broken.

roles.role_description: Each group winds wire around the nail, closes and opens the circuit, and records how many clips cling in each state.
Circulates to check winding technique and prompts groups to articulate what changes between the on and off states.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly connects this unit to the previous one — the compass deflection showed a magnetic field around a wire — and poses the new question: can we make a wire behave as a magnet strong enough to pick up objects?
Groups wind wire around the nail, connect to a cell, test attraction of clips, then open the circuit and observe clips falling.
Groups compare results across the class, noting that all nails attract clips only when current flows.
Teacher names the device an electromagnet and briefly connects it to the lifting magnet story that opened the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: In the previous unit students saw the magnetic effect as a deflection; this unit makes it tangible as an attracting force. The key misconception to address is that students sometimes believe the nail itself becomes permanently magnetic — make sure groups open the circuit and confirm that clips fall off. Ask groups to count clips to keep observations precise.

periods.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of the electromagnet
periods.activity_description: Students form a cylindrical coil on a paper tube, place compasses at both ends, and insert an iron nail into the core. They identify which end of the coil is the North pole and which is the South pole, and observe how the iron core changes magnetic strength.

roles.role_description: Groups construct the coil, insert the iron core, and use compasses at each end to determine and label the poles.
Guides groups to compare the compass readings at each end and asks probing questions about what the poles tell them about the electromagnet's nature.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the previous unit — the nail electromagnet attracted clips but its polarity was not examined — and asks whether an electromagnet has distinct poles like a bar magnet.
Groups build the coil on the paper cylinder, connect to a cell, and systematically test each end with a compass to determine North and South poles.
Groups insert the iron nail core and compare clip-pick-up count before and after insertion, recording their findings.
Class discussion: groups report their pole findings and core-effect observations; teacher formalises the two properties on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit moves students from simply observing a magnetic effect to classifying the electromagnet's properties alongside those of a bar magnet. A common confusion is that students think the compass needle's North-seeking end points toward the electromagnet's North pole — remind them that opposite poles attract, so the compass North points toward the electromagnet's South pole. The readiness signal for the next unit is that every group can correctly label both poles.

periods.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of the electromagnet
periods.activity_description: Students vary the number of cells and the number of coil turns, each time counting how many iron clips the electromagnet lifts. They record results in a table and identify which variable produces the greater change in strength.

roles.role_description: Each group systematically changes one variable at a time — number of cells, then number of turns — recording clip counts and identifying the trend.
Ensures groups change only one variable at a time and prompts them to articulate the relationship as a generalisation rather than a single observation.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reviews the poles activity from the previous unit and introduces the new inquiry question: what controls how strong an electromagnet is?
Groups conduct the controlled investigation, first varying cell count while keeping turns fixed, then varying turns while keeping cell count fixed.
Groups present their tables to the class; the teacher draws out the generalisation that both current magnitude and coil turns affect strength.
Teacher previews the next unit: if current direction changes, do the poles change too?

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the pole-identification work from the previous unit, this unit has students move from labelling properties to ranking them quantitatively. Watch for groups who change both variables simultaneously — prompt them to isolate variables before drawing conclusions. A quick check: ask a group to predict what would happen to clip count if they halved the number of turns.
homework: Sketch a bar graph of your group's clip-count data from today's investigation, labelling both axes and writing one sentence describing the trend you see.

periods.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of the electromagnet
periods.activity_description: Students reverse the connections of the battery in their electromagnet circuit and re-check the poles using compasses. They record whether the North and South poles swap positions and what this tells them about the relationship between current direction and pole identity.

roles.role_description: Groups reverse battery terminals, re-identify poles using compasses, and record the new pole positions alongside the original ones.
Prompts groups to compare their before-and-after pole tables and to state the relationship between current direction and pole orientation as a clear rule.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the previous unit's finding about strength and introduces the new question: does changing current direction change the poles?
Groups reverse battery connections, use compasses to re-determine poles, and record both configurations side by side.
Class shares findings and together states the rule: reversing current direction reverses the poles of the electromagnet.
Teacher connects this controllability to the industrial application coming in the next unit — switching, reversing, and lifting.

periods.teacher_notes: After the strength investigation, this unit completes the properties classification of the electromagnet by showing that polarity is also controllable. Students sometimes expect the deflection to be large and obvious; if their winding is loose the effect may appear weak — check that wire is tightly wound and connections are secure. Confirm understanding by asking each group to predict the new pole positions before they reverse the battery.

periods.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism and industrial application of electromagnets
periods.activity_description: Students examine how lifting electromagnets mounted on cranes use controllable magnetic force to pick up and release heavy metal objects in scrap yards and factories. They trace the cause-and-effect chain from current state to magnetic field to mechanical action to object release.

roles.role_description: Guides a structured explanation of the crane lifting electromagnet, drawing the cause-and-effect chain on the board and connecting each link to the properties established in earlier units.
Each student constructs their own cause-and-effect diagram in their notebook, then writes a two-sentence explanation of how a crane operator releases a held object.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by revisiting the chapter's opening scene — a lifting magnet at a science exhibition — and asks students why that magnet could release clips on command.
Teacher delivers a structured explanation of the crane electromagnet, linking current on/off, magnetic field presence/absence, and object hold/release.
Students individually draw and annotate a cause-and-effect chain diagram in their notebooks.
Students share diagrams in pairs, checking each other's causal links before a brief whole-class review.

periods.teacher_notes: In the previous three units students built and characterised the electromagnet; this unit asks them to apply that understanding to explain a real-world mechanism causally. A common gap is students stating that 'the magnet turns off' without explaining that the field disappears because current stops — push them to name the mechanism. The cause-and-effect diagram is the key artefact: it is the readiness signal that students can move from classification to explanation.

periods.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism and industrial application of electromagnets
periods.activity_description: Students examine the claim that Earth behaves as a magnet because of moving liquid iron in its core. They connect this to the compass deflection activity from the chapter's opening, explaining how a moving conductor generates a magnetic field at planetary scale.

roles.role_description: Each student reads the Step Further sidebar about Earth's magnetic field, then writes an explanation connecting Earth's liquid iron core to the magnetic effect established in the chapter.
Facilitates a brief discussion after individual reading, asking students to identify which principle from earlier units also explains Earth's magnetic behaviour.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the question: if a compass always points north, there must be something magnetic at Earth's pole — what could cause that?
Students read the sidebar on Earth's magnetic field and independently write a two-to-three sentence explanation linking core movement to magnetic field generation.
Class discussion: students share their explanations; teacher draws out the common principle — moving current (whether in a wire or liquid iron) produces a magnetic field.
Teacher signals the pivot: having explained the magnetic effect fully, the next unit opens a second effect of current — the heating effect.

periods.teacher_notes: After the crane application in the previous unit, this unit extends the causal explanation to a natural planetary phenomenon, deepening the mechanistic understanding of the magnetic effect. Students may struggle to see liquid iron as a 'current' — prompt them with the reminder that current is moving charges, and moving conducting material carries charges along. Check that students can articulate the common principle before the pivot to the heating effect begins.
materials: Chapter textbook (Step Further sidebar on Earth's magnetic field)

periods.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of electric current
periods.activity_description: A nichrome wire is connected in a simple circuit. Students touch the wire before and after current flows, observing that it becomes warm, and record how the warmth changes when a second cell is added. They identify that greater current produces greater heat.

roles.role_description: Groups connect the nichrome wire, carefully touch it before and after current flows with one cell, then repeat with two cells, recording warmth in each case.
Demonstrates safe touching technique, ensures groups record observations at each current level, and guides attention to the difference between one-cell and two-cell warmth.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the new strand by asking: we know current produces a magnetic effect — can it also produce another kind of effect? Students predict.
Groups conduct the observation with nichrome wire, carefully touching and recording warmth at one-cell and two-cell current levels.
Groups share observations; class notes that more current produces more heat and that the wire returns to room temperature when the circuit is opened.
Teacher introduces the term heating effect of electric current and names resistance as the mechanism linking current to heat.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the second major strand of the chapter — the heating effect — and students should see it as a parallel discovery to the magnetic effect they investigated in earlier units. The key misconception to address is that students sometimes expect all wires to heat equally; nichrome is chosen because it has high resistance — connect this to why heating elements in appliances are made of specific materials. Safety note: ensure students touch the wire only briefly and never when connected to more than two cells.
materials: Battery holder with one and two cells

periods.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of electric current
periods.activity_title: Resistance, Energy, and the Heating Mechanism
periods.activity_description: Students examine the causal mechanism of the heating effect: resistance opposes current flow and converts electrical energy into heat energy. They identify the factors that determine how much heat is generated — current magnitude, material, thickness, length, and duration.

roles.role_description: Delivers a structured explanation of the resistance-to-heat mechanism, writing the causal chain on the board and connecting each factor to its effect on heat produced.
Each student records the causal chain and lists all five factors affecting heat generation, then ranks them in their own words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the previous unit: students felt more heat with two cells — now ask what property of the wire caused it to heat at all.
Teacher explains the resistance mechanism: current meets opposition in the conductor, and this converts electrical energy into heat; students record the causal chain.
Teacher walks through the five factors — current magnitude, material, thickness, length, duration — with a brief illustrative example for each; students note all five.
Quick pair-share: one student explains the mechanism to their partner without notes; teacher circulates to check accuracy.

periods.teacher_notes: Following the hands-on observation in the previous unit, this unit gives students the conceptual vocabulary to explain what they felt. A common confusion is conflating 'resistance' with 'a block' that stops current entirely — clarify that resistance slows current and converts energy without stopping it. The pair-share at the close is a useful readiness check before moving to applications.

periods.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of electric current
periods.activity_description: Students examine common household appliances — room heaters, electric stoves, kettles, irons, immersion rods, and hair dryers — and identify that each contains a heating element made of a high-resistance wire or coil. They classify appliances by intended use of the heating effect.

roles.role_description: Groups receive a list of appliances and classify them by the purpose of their heating element, then identify what property of the element each appliance relies on.
Introduces the concept of a heating element, then circulates as groups work, asking probing questions about which factors from the previous unit each appliance exploits.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the previous unit's five factors and asks: where do we deliberately use the heating effect in daily life?
Groups classify the given list of appliances by purpose — warming, cooking, drying, pressing — and identify the role of the heating element in each.
Groups share classifications; class builds a common table on the board linking appliance, purpose, and the relevant heating-effect factor.
Teacher flags the dual nature of heating: useful in appliances, but also a source of energy loss and fire risk in transmission — preview for the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: After establishing the mechanism in the previous unit, this unit consolidates it through classification of real-world applications. Students sometimes think only appliances with visible glowing wires (such as room heaters) use the heating effect — point out that a kettle and iron also rely on it even though the element is hidden. The classification table is a good formative check on whether students have correctly linked the mechanism to its applications.
materials: List of household appliances (printed or written on board)

periods.stage_label: Explain the source of current: cells and batteries
periods.activity_description: Students construct a Voltaic cell using a lemon, a copper wire, and an iron nail as electrodes, and connect the cell to a LED to confirm that the lemon-juice electrolyte drives a current. They observe that the chemical reaction between the electrodes and electrolyte is the source of electrical energy.

roles.role_description: Groups build the lemon cell, connect it to the LED, observe light emission, and record which electrode is positive and which is negative.
Explains the role of the electrolyte as a medium for the chemical reaction and prompts groups to connect the light emission to the concept that current requires a source of energy.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by asking: every circuit we have built uses a battery — but what is inside a battery that produces current? Students make predictions.
Groups construct the lemon Voltaic cell, connect to the LED, and record their observations including electrode identity and light emission.
Groups share results; teacher introduces the term electrolyte and explains that the chemical reaction between two different metal electrodes and the electrolyte drives current.
Teacher connects the lemon cell to the historical story of Galvani and Volta, briefly narrating how the discovery was made.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the third strand of the chapter — the source of current — making it clear to students that the battery is not a mystery box but a device with a specific chemical mechanism. A common confusion is that students think any liquid will act as an electrolyte; clarify that the electrolyte must be a weak acid or salt solution that supports the chemical reaction between the two different metals. Check that every group's LED actually lights before drawing conclusions — dim or no light usually means poor electrode contact.

periods.stage_label: Explain the source of current: cells and batteries
periods.activity_title: From Voltaic Cell to Dry Cell
periods.activity_description: Students examine the structure of a dry cell — zinc container, carbon rod, paste electrolyte — and compare it to the Voltaic cell they built. They identify why the paste electrolyte makes the dry cell more practical and portable, and why it is a single-use device.

roles.role_description: Presents the dry cell structure with a labelled diagram, drawing explicit comparisons to the lemon Voltaic cell and explaining why portability depends on the solid-paste electrolyte.
Each student draws and labels the dry cell structure in their notebook and writes a comparison sentence identifying one advantage of the dry cell over the Voltaic cell.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the lemon Voltaic cell from the previous unit and asks what the practical problem would be with using a liquid electrolyte in a portable device.
Teacher presents the dry cell structure with a diagram; students copy and label the diagram in their notebooks.
Students individually write a comparison sentence, then share with the class; teacher formalises the single-use limitation.
Teacher poses the next question: if a dry cell is single-use, what is the alternative for devices we use repeatedly?

periods.teacher_notes: After students built a working Voltaic cell in the previous unit, this unit uses that experience to make the dry cell's design logic obvious — the paste electrolyte solves the portability problem. A misconception to watch for is that students think the dry cell contains no liquid at all; clarify that the electrolyte is a moist paste, not a fully dry substance. The comparison sentence is a concise formative check on whether students have grasped the design rationale.
materials: Labelled diagram of dry cell structure (drawn on board or provided on sheet)

periods.stage_label: Explain the source of current: cells and batteries
periods.activity_description: Students examine rechargeable batteries — from watches and phones to laptops and electric vehicles — identifying the trade-offs of rechargeability versus single-use and the environmental and safety responsibilities that come with battery disposal.

roles.role_description: Groups discuss a set of scenarios involving battery choice and disposal, deciding which battery type is most appropriate for each and justifying their reasoning.

Introduces rechargeable battery types including lithium-ion, facilitates the group scenario discussion, and ensures students connect disposal responsibility to the toxic materials inside spent batteries.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by listing devices from the chapter — watch, phone, laptop, electric vehicle — and asks why a single-use dry cell would be impractical for each.
Groups work through a set of battery-choice scenarios — wristwatch, school laptop, city bus — justifying their choice of rechargeable or single-use and explaining the trade-off.
Groups share decisions; class discusses the safety note about dead batteries containing acids and toxic metals requiring e-waste disposal.
Teacher previews that the next unit will introduce a further property of electricity — electromagnetic induction — as a bridge concept.

periods.teacher_notes: Following the structural comparison of Voltaic and dry cells, this unit extends the strand to rechargeable batteries and disposal, requiring students to apply trade-off reasoning rather than just recall structures. A common gap is students assuming rechargeable batteries last indefinitely — clarify that they too wear out after many charge-discharge cycles. The scenario exercise works well when groups are challenged to defend their choice against a classmate's objection.
materials: Scenario cards or list of battery-choice scenarios (printed or on board)
homework: Choose one battery-powered device you use at home and write two sentences explaining which battery type it uses and why that choice makes sense given the device's use pattern.

periods.stage_label: Integrate and apply: connecting both effects and their energy sources to new contexts
periods.activity_description: Students examine a set of novel scenarios — a hospital sorting scrap metal, a remote weather station needing heat and signal transmission, an electric vehicle charging — and determine which effect of current (magnetic, heating, or both) is at work, tracing the causal chain from battery source through effect to function.

roles.role_description: Groups analyse each scenario, identify which effect of current is operating and which type of energy source is supplying it, then write a causal explanation connecting source to effect to outcome.
Presents the scenarios, circulates to ensure groups are drawing on both the magnetic and heating effect strands, and prompts groups to justify their battery-type choices.

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames the unit as an integration challenge: can you use everything from this chapter to explain a situation you have not seen before?
Groups work through the scenario set, producing a causal explanation for each that names the effect, the mechanism, and the appropriate energy source.
Groups share one scenario explanation each; class discusses and refines the causal chains together.
Teacher notes that the final unit will draw the whole chapter together across all three strands into a unified picture.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the culmination of the teaching arc across units 1–13 and asks students to work across all three strands simultaneously for the first time. Watch for groups who treat the two effects as entirely separate — the goal is integration, so push them to consider whether both effects could be relevant in a single device. A group that can write a causal chain naming battery type, current, resistance or magnetic field, and outcome is demonstrating the chapter's dissolution-test operation.
materials: Scenario cards or list printed on board

periods.stage_label: Integrate and apply: connecting both effects and their energy sources to new contexts
periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: One Current, Three Strands
periods.activity_description: Students reconstruct the chapter's three interconnected strands — the magnetic effect, the heating effect, and the sources of current — as a single unified concept map, then use it to explain how a complex device such as an electric bell or industrial furnace depends on all three ideas working together.

roles.role_description: Each student builds a concept map connecting the three strands — magnetic effect, heating effect, and cell/battery source — and annotates each link with a causal mechanism drawn from the chapter.
Poses the synthesis question, circulates to probe the quality of causal links on individual maps, and facilitates a whole-class comparison of maps at the close.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the synthesis question: electricity produces a magnetic effect and a heating effect, and both require a source — how do all three fit into one picture?
Students individually construct a concept map with three strands as nodes, linking them with annotated causal arrows that name the mechanism at each connection.
Students pair up to compare maps, identifying any causal links their partner has that they missed and discussing whether the links are accurate.
Teacher facilitates a brief whole-class closing discussion, asking two or three students to read one causal link each, and draws the chapter's unifying idea on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the whole-chapter synthesis unit: the class has covered the full content of this chapter and has reached the point of applying and integrating both the magnetic and heating effects together with their energy sources. Pose the synthesis question broadly, relying on the concepts themselves. The strength of a student's concept map lies in the quality of the causal annotations — a map with many nodes but weak or missing annotations is a weaker response than a simpler map with precise causal language on every link.
materials: Blank paper or large sheets for concept maps

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of electric current
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe compass deflection under a current-carrying wire and build a nail electromagnet, recording that the magnetic effect appears with current and disappears without it.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe, with evidence from their own observations, that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that disappears when the current stops.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of the electromagnet
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students identify the North and South poles of a coil electromagnet, investigate how current magnitude and coil turns affect strength, and verify that reversing current direction reverses the poles.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify an electromagnet's properties — polarity, strength dependence on current and turns, and pole reversibility — and distinguish them from those of a permanent bar magnet.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism and industrial application of electromagnets
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct causal chains explaining how the crane lifting electromagnet works and how Earth's magnetic field arises from the same principle of current-produced magnetic fields.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain causally how switching current on and off controls the magnetic force of an industrial lifting electromagnet, and connect this same mechanism to Earth's magnetic behaviour.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of electric current
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe that a nichrome wire heats when current flows, explain the resistance mechanism that converts electrical energy to heat, and classify household appliances by their use of the heating effect.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain the heating effect of electric current by identifying resistance as the converting mechanism and classify real appliances by which factor of heat generation they exploit.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain the source of current: cells and batteries
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students build a lemon Voltaic cell, compare it to the dry cell's structure, and evaluate rechargeable battery trade-offs and disposal responsibilities.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain how a Voltaic cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy through an electrolyte and two different metal electrodes, and compare single-use and rechargeable cells by trade-offs of design and disposal.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Integrate and apply: connecting both effects and their energy sources to new contexts
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students analyse novel scenarios and build a whole-chapter concept map that traces the causal chain from energy source through current to both the magnetic and heating effects simultaneously.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe how electricity produces magnetic and heating effects by constructing causal explanations that connect the appropriate energy source (cell or battery) through current to each effect, and apply this reasoning to unfamiliar contexts.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe, with evidence from their own observations, that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that disappears when the current stops.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A magnetic compass is placed directly under a wire connected in a circuit. When the switch is closed, the compass needle deflects. When the switch is opened, the needle returns to its original position. What does this observation show about the wire?

options.label: A
options.text: The compass needle deflects because the wire blocks the Earth's magnetic field.

options.label: B
options.text: The magnetic effect is caused by the heat produced in the wire when current flows.

options.label: C
options.text: The wire becomes permanently magnetic when current flows through it.

options.label: D
options.text: The wire produces a magnetic field only when current flows through it.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student confuses the electromagnet's temporary field with permanent magnetism — a direct misconception addressed in the nail electromagnet activity.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option suggests the student has not understood that the compass deflects toward the new field rather than away from a blocked one — a confusion about how magnetic fields interact.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a conflation of the magnetic effect and the heating effect, treating them as the same phenomenon rather than two distinct effects of current.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who observed the compass activity directly can draw on sensory memory; students who find abstract reasoning easier may approach this through the on/off logic of the switch controlling the field.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe, with evidence from their own observations, that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that disappears when the current stops.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wraps insulated wire around an iron nail and connects it to a battery. Iron clips cling to the nail while the circuit is closed. When the circuit is opened, the clips fall off. Which term correctly names this device?

options.label: A
options.text: Bar magnet

options.label: B
options.text: Electromagnet

options.label: C
options.text: Heating element

options.label: D
options.text: Voltaic cell

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student has not registered that the magnetic effect is temporary and current-controlled — the defining distinction between an electromagnet and a bar magnet.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student is confusing the source of current (the cell) with the device that uses it to produce a magnetic effect — a chapter-internal concept confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student is associating the current-carrying wire only with the heating effect, not recognising that the same wire can produce a magnetic effect depending on context.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who need concrete grounding can focus on the clips-cling-and-fall observation as the defining behaviour; students who prefer definitional thinking can approach it through the criterion of current-controlled magnetism.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of the electromagnet
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify an electromagnet's properties — polarity, strength dependence on current and turns, and pole reversibility — and distinguish them from those of a permanent bar magnet.

competency.competency_text: Properties of natural and artificial magnets; Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: A student increases the number of turns in an electromagnet's coil while keeping the battery the same. What change, if any, will the student observe?

options.label: A
options.text: No change will occur because only the battery determines electromagnet strength.

options.label: B
options.text: The electromagnet will no longer have distinct North and South poles.

options.label: C
options.text: The electromagnet will pick up more iron clips than before.

options.label: D
options.text: The electromagnet's poles will reverse.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option confuses the strength-variable investigation with the pole-reversal activity — two distinct properties of the electromagnet conflated into one.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option suggests the student believes polarity depends on coil geometry, not understanding that poles are a stable property of the electromagnet regardless of turn count.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals a misconception that only current magnitude (set by the battery) affects strength, failing to generalise that coil turns are also an independent strength variable.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who retained their data table from the investigation can reason from recorded evidence; students who think in structural terms can reason from the idea that more turns create more loops of current.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of the electromagnet
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify an electromagnet's properties — polarity, strength dependence on current and turns, and pole reversibility — and distinguish them from those of a permanent bar magnet.

competency.competency_text: Properties of natural and artificial magnets; Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: A student connects a compass to each end of a current-carrying coil and finds that one end is the North pole and the other is the South pole. The student then reverses the battery connections. What will happen to the poles?

options.label: A
options.text: Both ends will become North poles.

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing will change because the coil and iron core are unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: The North pole and South pole will swap positions.

options.label: D
options.text: The poles will disappear because the current direction has changed.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student does not understand that a magnet must have two opposite poles — a direct misconception about the dipole nature of all magnets including electromagnets.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option confuses pole reversal with pole disappearance, suggesting the student thinks changing current direction stops the magnetic effect entirely rather than reversing its orientation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option shows the student has not connected current direction to pole identity — they recall that the coil and core determine the magnetic field but have not grasped that current direction determines polarity.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who found the physical reversal memorable can recall the before-and-after compass positions; students who reason analytically can think through the direction of current flow through each loop.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of the electromagnet
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify an electromagnet's properties — polarity, strength dependence on current and turns, and pole reversibility — and distinguish them from those of a permanent bar magnet.

competency.competency_text: Properties of natural and artificial magnets; Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'An electromagnet is just like a bar magnet — it has North and South poles and can attract iron.' Another student disagrees, saying they are not alike. Give two properties that make an electromagnet different from a bar magnet.
expected_elements: An electromagnet's magnetic effect exists only while current flows; a bar magnet's effect is permanent.
The poles of an electromagnet can be reversed by reversing the direction of current; a bar magnet's poles cannot be switched.
The strength of an electromagnet can be changed by varying current or number of coil turns; a bar magnet's strength is fixed.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who reason from their construction experience can point to the switch as the mechanism for the temporary nature; students who approached the classification more analytically can draw on their recorded comparison table of properties.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism and industrial application of electromagnets
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain causally how switching current on and off controls the magnetic force of an industrial lifting electromagnet, and connect this same mechanism to Earth's magnetic behaviour.

competency.competency_text: Properties of natural and artificial magnets; Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: A crane operator uses a lifting electromagnet to move scrap metal. To release the metal, the operator switches off the current. Why does switching off the current cause the metal to be released?

options.label: A
options.text: Switching off the current reduces the number of coil turns, weakening the magnet.

options.label: B
options.text: Without current, no magnetic field is produced, so there is no force holding the metal.

options.label: C
options.text: Without current, the electromagnet's poles reverse, pushing the metal away.

options.label: D
options.text: Without current, the iron core becomes a permanent magnet that repels the scrap metal.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option confuses the mechanism of release (field disappears) with the pole-reversal property, applying a different electromagnet property to the wrong situation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals a misconception that switching off the current physically changes the coil geometry — the student has not grasped that the field is produced by current flow, not by the presence of turns alone.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option indicates a direct misconception about the iron core: the student believes it retains permanent magnetism after current stops, which directly contradicts the temporary-field property of an electromagnet.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who remember the clips-fall-off observation can ground their reasoning there; students who prefer a step-by-step mechanical approach can trace the causal chain: current off → no field → no force → release.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism and industrial application of electromagnets
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain causally how switching current on and off controls the magnetic force of an industrial lifting electromagnet, and connect this same mechanism to Earth's magnetic behaviour.

competency.competency_text: Properties of natural and artificial magnets; Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: Earth behaves like a giant magnet, producing a magnetic field that compass needles respond to. According to what the chapter explains, what is the source of Earth's magnetic field?

options.label: A
options.text: A large bar magnet located at Earth's geographic North Pole.

options.label: B
options.text: Movement of liquid iron in Earth's core, which acts like a current-carrying conductor.

options.label: C
options.text: The heating of Earth's mantle, which produces heat energy that converts to magnetic energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The rotation of Earth's solid outer crust, which generates static electricity.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the classic naive conception that Earth's magnetism comes from a physical magnet inside it, rather than understanding the current-production mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has partially connected motion to electricity but applied it to the wrong layer of Earth and confused static electricity with current-generated magnetism.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option conflates the heating effect with the magnetic effect — a chapter-internal confusion between two distinct effects of current.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find analogical reasoning accessible can connect the liquid iron to the wire they used: both are conductors in motion. Students who respond better to structural explanations can focus on the chapter's direct statement about the liquid iron core.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain the causal mechanism and industrial application of electromagnets
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain causally how switching current on and off controls the magnetic force of an industrial lifting electromagnet, and connect this same mechanism to Earth's magnetic behaviour.

competency.competency_text: Properties of natural and artificial magnets; Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: In a scrap yard, a crane operator lifts a heavy iron beam using an electromagnet. Describe, step by step, the causal chain from the moment the operator switches on the current to the moment the beam is held in the air. Use at least three steps in your answer.
expected_elements: Current flows through the coil of the electromagnet.
The current-carrying coil produces a magnetic field around it.
The magnetic field exerts a force on the iron beam, attracting it.
The beam is held in the air as long as the current continues to flow.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who drew a cause-and-effect diagram can work from that memory; students who prefer verbal reasoning can narrate the steps as a story about what the operator and the magnet do in sequence.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain the heating effect of electric current by identifying resistance as the converting mechanism and classify real appliances by which factor of heat generation they exploit.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A student connects a nichrome wire in a simple circuit and observes that the wire becomes warm when current flows. What is the reason the wire heats up?

options.label: A
options.text: The nichrome wire has high resistance, which opposes current flow and converts electrical energy into heat energy.

options.label: B
options.text: The nichrome wire heats up because it is made of a special material that attracts heat from the battery.

options.label: C
options.text: The nichrome wire produces a magnetic field that generates heat in the surrounding air.

options.label: D
options.text: The nichrome wire stores electrical energy and releases it as heat when the circuit is opened.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option conflates the heating effect with the magnetic effect — the student attributes the warmth to a field rather than to resistance, showing the two effects have not been distinguished.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals a misconception about when heat is released — the student imagines a storage-and-release model, not understanding that heat is produced continuously while current flows.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option shows the student has not grasped the mechanism at all, attributing the heating to an undefined material property rather than to the resistance-conversion process.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who retained the tactile observation of wire warmth increasing with more cells can reason from that experience; students who prefer mechanistic explanations can work from the resistance-to-heat energy-conversion chain.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain the heating effect of electric current by identifying resistance as the converting mechanism and classify real appliances by which factor of heat generation they exploit.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: An electric iron is designed to heat a flat metal plate to press clothes. Which factor of heat generation is most directly exploited in the design of an iron's heating element?

options.label: A
options.text: The length and material of the heating wire, chosen to produce the right amount of heat.

options.label: B
options.text: The number of coil turns in the heating element, which determines the magnetic field strength.

options.label: C
options.text: The type of electrolyte inside the heating element that reacts chemically to produce heat.

options.label: D
options.text: The voltage of the household supply alone, regardless of the material of the heating element.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option imports the electromagnet strand into the heating appliance context — the student confuses coil turns as a strength variable for electromagnets with how a heating element is designed.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option imports the cell/battery strand — the student confuses the electrolyte as a heat source, mixing up the source-of-current strand with the heating effect strand.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has only partially absorbed the five factors, accepting that current (driven by voltage) matters while overlooking that material and length are independently designed into the element.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who recall the appliance classification activity can approach this by thinking about which design decision the engineer controls; students who prefer principle-based reasoning can work from the five factors list.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain the heating effect of electric current by identifying resistance as the converting mechanism and classify real appliances by which factor of heat generation they exploit.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: The heating effect of electric current is described as having a 'dual nature' in everyday life. Explain what this means by giving one example of the heating effect being useful and one example of it being a problem.
expected_elements: The heating effect is useful in appliances such as electric stoves, kettles, irons, room heaters, immersion rods, or hair dryers, where electrical energy is deliberately converted to heat.
The heating effect is a problem when it causes energy loss during electricity transmission, overheating of devices, melting of plastic components, or risk of fire.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who draw on daily life experience will find the useful example easy; students who prefer to reason from the mechanism can think about what happens when heat appears where it is not wanted — wires in walls, transmission lines.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain the source of current: cells and batteries
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain how a Voltaic cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy through an electrolyte and two different metal electrodes, and compare single-use and rechargeable cells by trade-offs of design and disposal.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: In a Voltaic cell, a chemical reaction between two different metal electrodes and the electrolyte produces electricity. What happens to the cell over time as the circuit remains connected?

options.label: A
options.text: The cell recharges itself from the surrounding air, allowing it to produce current indefinitely.

options.label: B
options.text: The chemicals are consumed by the reaction, and the cell eventually becomes dead.

options.label: C
options.text: The electrodes gain mass as the reaction deposits material on them, increasing the current.

options.label: D
options.text: The electrolyte evaporates, causing the cell to stop producing current.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has partially grasped that the liquid is important but has confused the electrolyte's role — it is consumed chemically, not evaporated physically.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals a misconception about the direction of the reaction, imagining material is added rather than consumed — a confusion about what 'chemical reaction' means in this context.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student has confused the Voltaic cell with a rechargeable battery, not distinguishing between single-use and rechargeable designs.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who built the lemon cell can reason from the observation that the lemon juice becomes less effective over time; students who prefer structural reasoning can work from the principle that chemical reactions consume reactants.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain the source of current: cells and batteries
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain how a Voltaic cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy through an electrolyte and two different metal electrodes, and compare single-use and rechargeable cells by trade-offs of design and disposal.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A dry cell and a Voltaic cell both produce electric current from a chemical reaction. What is the key structural difference that makes the dry cell more practical for portable devices?

options.label: A
options.text: The dry cell can be recharged indefinitely, while the Voltaic cell is always single-use.

options.label: B
options.text: The dry cell generates more current than the Voltaic cell because its carbon rod has lower resistance.

options.label: C
options.text: The dry cell uses a thick moist paste as its electrolyte instead of a liquid, making it portable and leak-resistant.

options.label: D
options.text: The dry cell uses two identical metal electrodes, while the Voltaic cell uses two different metals.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has confused the electrode-identity criterion — both cells require two different metals; the structural difference is in the electrolyte, not the electrodes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option conflates the heating-effect strand (resistance in a wire) with cell structure, misapplying the resistance concept to the electrode rod in a battery.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals a confusion between the dry cell and rechargeable batteries — the dry cell is also a single-use device, but the student believes portability implies rechargeability.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who built the lemon Voltaic cell with liquid lemon juice can contrast it directly with the paste description; students who reason from the design problem can think about why a liquid electrolyte would be inconvenient in a pocket device.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain the source of current: cells and batteries
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain how a Voltaic cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy through an electrolyte and two different metal electrodes, and compare single-use and rechargeable cells by trade-offs of design and disposal.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A student's school is deciding whether to use single-use dry cells or rechargeable batteries in its science equipment. Give two reasons why rechargeable batteries might be the better choice, and one reason why they still need to be disposed of carefully when worn out.
expected_elements: Rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused multiple times, reducing waste and cost over time compared to single-use dry cells.
Rechargeable batteries reduce the frequency of replacement, making them more practical for equipment used repeatedly.
Even rechargeable batteries contain acids and toxic metals and must be disposed of at e-waste recycling facilities when they no longer hold a charge.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who reasoned through the scenario activity can draw on that decision-making process; students who prefer cost-benefit reasoning can frame the trade-offs explicitly in economic and environmental terms.

assessment_items.stage_label: Integrate and apply: connecting both effects and their energy sources to new contexts
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe how electricity produces magnetic and heating effects by constructing causal explanations that connect the appropriate energy source (cell or battery) through current to each effect, and apply this reasoning to unfamiliar contexts.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: An electric bell contains a coil of wire wrapped around an iron core. When the bell is connected to a battery and the switch is pressed, the iron core becomes magnetic and pulls a metal striker to ring the bell. When the striker touches the bell, the circuit briefly breaks and the core loses its magnetism, allowing the striker to return — and the cycle repeats. Which effect of electric current is operating in the electric bell, and what type of energy source drives it?

options.label: A
options.text: Both the heating and magnetic effects together; the coil heats up and becomes magnetic simultaneously.

options.label: B
options.text: The heating effect; the bell is powered by a Voltaic cell with liquid electrolyte.

options.label: C
options.text: The magnetic effect; but no energy source is needed because the iron core is a permanent magnet.

options.label: D
options.text: The magnetic effect; the bell is powered by a cell or battery that supplies current to the coil.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option shows the student has confused the effect (magnetic, which makes the striker move) with the heating effect, and has also not applied the trade-off reasoning about when a Voltaic cell is practical.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals that the student has not yet fully distinguished the two effects as operating independently — they assume any energised coil simultaneously produces both, rather than recognising that the primary function here is magnetic.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option demonstrates the persistent misconception about iron cores retaining permanent magnetism — the student has not applied the temporary-field property of the electromagnet to this new device context.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who approach this analytically can trace the cycle step by step; students who reason by analogy can compare the bell's coil-and-core to the nail electromagnet they built and ask whether the same switch-on/switch-off logic applies.

assessment_items.stage_label: Integrate and apply: connecting both effects and their energy sources to new contexts
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe how electricity produces magnetic and heating effects by constructing causal explanations that connect the appropriate energy source (cell or battery) through current to each effect, and apply this reasoning to unfamiliar contexts.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: High-voltage transmission lines carry electricity over long distances. Engineers notice that the lines get warm during transmission and that some electrical energy is lost as heat. Which concept from this chapter explains this energy loss, and what property of the wire causes it?

options.label: A
options.text: The heating effect; the wire heats up because the electrolyte in the power station's battery releases heat into the circuit.

options.label: B
options.text: The heating effect; the wire's resistance converts some electrical energy into heat as current flows through it.

options.label: C
options.text: The magnetic effect; the current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field that radiates energy away from the wire.

options.label: D
options.text: The magnetic effect; the wire generates a magnetic field that interacts with Earth's magnetic field, causing energy loss.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option conflates the two effects — the student identifies that the wire carries current and that a field is produced, but misattributes the energy loss to field radiation rather than resistance-based heat conversion.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option imports the battery strand incorrectly into the transmission context — the student incorrectly places the source of heat in the electrolyte rather than in the wire's resistance.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has connected Earth's magnetic field from the chapter but misapplied it as an energy-loss mechanism, combining two correct facts (wire produces field; Earth has field) into an incorrect causal claim.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who remember touching the warm nichrome wire can connect that observation directly to transmission lines; students who prefer causal chain reasoning can trace current → resistance → heat → energy loss step by step.

assessment_items.stage_label: Integrate and apply: connecting both effects and their energy sources to new contexts
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe how electricity produces magnetic and heating effects by constructing causal explanations that connect the appropriate energy source (cell or battery) through current to each effect, and apply this reasoning to unfamiliar contexts.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A hospital uses an electromagnet on a crane to sort and lift scrap iron from a mixed pile of waste materials. The maintenance team suggests replacing the electromagnet with a powerful permanent bar magnet to save energy. Evaluate this suggestion: explain whether it would work, and identify at least two properties of an electromagnet that a permanent magnet cannot provide in this application.
look_for: The student correctly identifies that a permanent magnet would attract iron continuously and cannot be switched off, making it impossible to release objects on command — unlike the electromagnet whose field disappears when current is stopped.
The student names the controllable nature of the electromagnet's field (on/off via current) as an essential property for the sorting and releasing function.

The student identifies at least one further property: the electromagnet's strength can be varied (by changing current or coil turns), allowing different loads to be handled, or its poles can be reversed, which a bar magnet cannot do.
The student's evaluation is explicitly structured as a judgement — not just a description of electromagnet properties — stating whether the suggestion would work and why.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find evaluative writing challenging can structure their response as: 'It would/would not work because...' followed by two numbered property comparisons. Students who are comfortable with extended argument can develop the evaluation more fully by considering each operational requirement of the sorting application in turn.

assessment_items.stage_label: Integrate and apply: connecting both effects and their energy sources to new contexts
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe how electricity produces magnetic and heating effects by constructing causal explanations that connect the appropriate energy source (cell or battery) through current to each effect, and apply this reasoning to unfamiliar contexts.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Device | Main effect of current used | Causal mechanism (fill in) | Energy source type | Why this source suits the device
Electric bell | | | |
Electric room heater | | | |
Lifting electromagnet on a factory crane | | | |
Laptop battery-powered electromagnet in a speaker | | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each device: (1) identify whether the magnetic effect, heating effect, or both are at work; (2) describe the causal mechanism that produces that effect — naming resistance, magnetic field, or both as appropriate; (3) identify the type of energy source (single-use cell, rechargeable battery, or mains supply where applicable); (4) explain in one sentence why that energy source suits the device's use pattern.
assessment_items.scaffold: Start with the device you know best. For the causal mechanism column, use the chain: current flows → [resistance / coil + iron core] → [heat energy / magnetic field] → [function]. For the energy source column, think about whether the device is used once, repeatedly, or continuously. Your explanation in the last column should connect the source's trade-offs (single-use vs rechargeable vs mains) to the device's actual use.
format_of_output: Completed table with all four columns filled for all four devices
Each mechanism description names at least one physical property (resistance or magnetic field)
Each energy source explanation links the source type to the device's use pattern

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Final Stage implied LO requires students to connect both effects and their energy sources in a single integrated act of reasoning; a classification-with-justification table is the most natural vehicle because it forces explicit parallel comparison across all three strands of the chapter for multiple devices simultaneously.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can simultaneously apply the magnetic-effect mechanism, the heating-effect mechanism, and cell/battery trade-off reasoning to novel device contexts — the full dissolution-test operation.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The four-column structure mirrors the chapter's three strands plus the integration link; a student who fills only the first two columns has shown strand knowledge but not integration. The energy source explanation column is the key integration indicator — it requires the student to connect all three strands in one sentence per device.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses name specific mechanisms (resistance converts electrical energy to heat; current through coil produces magnetic field) and connect the energy source choice explicitly to a feature of the device's use (used repeatedly → rechargeable; continuous industrial use → mains). Weak responses name the effect without the mechanism (it heats up) and describe the source without justification (it uses a battery).
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the full table demanding can complete the two devices they know best first and use those as a template for the others. Students who work faster can be asked to add a fifth row for a device of their own choice.
